GT assumes that social phenomena like learning can be understood by systematically gathering and analyzing data. Our study focused on tracking changes in students' academic performance over time and the factors that influenced those changes.

The constant comparison method—examining data as it was collected—was central to our analysis. We compared each student’s performance in one year to the next and traced the effects of interventions (like tutoring or mentoring) on their academic trajectory. This allowed us to identify patterns or "categories" that emerged across the entire dataset.

We also used the selective coding method to refine our categories by focusing on the most relevant data. For example, we tagged which interventions were most effective and which student characteristics (e.g., socioeconomic status, prior academic performance) were most predictive of success.

In sum, Grounded Theory helped us uncover how specific interventions and contextual factors interact over time to shape student outcomes.
